summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping uses a Diameter Network Access Server to interact with Diameter servers, so home agent address, home address and security details can be provided dynamically through existing AAA infrastructure. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A traveling device needs a home address and a key before it can start. This lets it get them from the same login system the network already uses.

questions: diameter nas to aaa for mipv6
how does a mobile node get a home agent
subtitle: How a network access server and a Diameter server hand a Mobile IPv6 device its home agent during login.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv6 node needs a home agent address, a home link prefix and related details before it can work, and RFC 3775 expects them to be configured by hand. That is a burden and cannot balance load or pick a nearby home agent.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5447 defines new Diameter attribute-value pairs (AVPs) so the network access server and the Diameter server can exchange home agent information and capabilities during network access authentication.
tldr.outcome: The AAA system used for access login can assign the home agent dynamically. The RFC leaves the security association between node and home agent out of scope.

today: RFC 5447 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends Diameter with the AVPs needed for integrated-scenario Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping.

sections.title: Why Bootstrap Mobile IPv6 with AAA
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) lets a mobile node (MN) register its current point of attachment, the care-of address, with a home agent (HA). To register, the node needs the home link prefix, the HA address, its home address or addresses, the home link prefix length and security-association information.

All of this could be configured statically. The RFC points out that static provisioning is an administrative burden, and that it does not address load balancing, failover, opportunistic home link assignment or assigning a local HA close to the node. It also reacts poorly to sudden topology changes.

The alternative is to reuse the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) infrastructure that already handles access authentication, and let a Diameter server return some or all of these parameters.
sections.eli5: Writing down your home base by hand is a chore and does not help if the base is busy or far away. It is easier to ask the same office that already checks your ID.

sections.title: The Integrated Scenario
sections.content:
The RFC covers the integrated scenario, where the mobility service and the network access service are authorized by the same entity, so bootstrapping happens as part of network access authentication. (In the split scenario they are authorized by different entities.) The relevant interface is the one between the Network Access Server (NAS), acting as a Diameter client, and the home AAA (HAAA) Diameter server. Local or visited Diameter proxies may sit in between.

While the Diameter server authenticates and authorizes the user for network access, it also decides whether the user may use MIPv6. Based on that and the user's policy profile, it may return several bootstrapping parameters to the NAS. The interface is not tied to DHCPv6 as the only way to pass them on to the mobile node.

Creating the security association between the node and its home agent is out of scope. It happens after the procedures described here.
sections.eli5: When you log in at the front desk, the desk can also hand you a card that names your home base. Setting up your secret handshake with that base comes later.

sections.title: The New AVPs
sections.content:
RFC 5447 does not define a new Diameter application. It defines AVPs that can be used with any present or future application where the command ABNF permits. The examples reuse the Diameter EAP application from RFC 4072.

  • MIP6-Agent-Info (code 486, Grouped) carries what is needed to assign an HA. It MUST contain a MIP-Home-Agent-Address, a MIP-Home-Agent-Host, or both. It may also hold a MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix. Up to two addresses are allowed, which suits an HA with both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses.
  • MIP-Home-Agent-Address (code 334, Address) holds an IPv6 or IPv4 address of the HA. The server may pick an HA near the point of attachment or to share load.
  • MIP-Home-Agent-Host (code 348, Grouped) holds the Destination-Realm and Destination-Host of the HA, adding a level of indirection through DNS. It is RECOMMENDED that the host identify exactly one HA, and that this AVP is always included.
  • MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix (code 125, OctetString) holds a one-octet prefix length followed by a 16-octet prefix, with the trailing bits set to zero.

If both address and host are present, the address SHOULD take precedence, because it points to a specific HA while the host may point to a group. The NAS or proxies may attach MIP6-Agent-Info to a request as a hint of a locally assigned HA, and a message can carry several instances.
sections.eli5: The memo adds a few new boxes to the usual forms. One box names the home base, one names the address, and one holds the street prefix for your home network.

sections.title: The Feature Vector and Local Home Agents
sections.content:
The MIP6-Feature-Vector AVP (code 124, Unsigned64) is a 64-bit flags field of capabilities. Sending and receiving the value 0 MUST be supported. The NAS may include it to advertise capabilities, and the server may include it to say which of those are supported or authorized.

Two flags are defined. MIP6_INTEGRATED (0x0000000000000001) says integrated-scenario bootstrapping is supported. LOCAL_HOME_AGENT_ASSIGNMENT (0x0000000000000002) in a request asks for a local HA outside the home realm, and in an answer means the server authorizes local assignment.

The RFC gives tables of request and answer combinations. For instance, a request with the local bit clear means the access provider cannot assign a local HA, and any HA info must be ignored. In an answer with the local bit clear and a home-network HA, the server assigns the HA and a local one is not allowed. A NAS should expect to receive several MIP6-Agent-Info AVPs.
sections.eli5: A checklist of switches tells the other side what you can do. One switch means you can do this whole process, and another means you can offer a nearby home base.

sections.title: Worked Message Flows
sections.content:
Three examples show home agent assignment using Diameter-EAP messages.

  • Assignment by the NAS: the request sets both flags and carries a proposed HA address. The server accepts by returning the local flag with MIP6_INTEGRATED.
  • Assignment by the Diameter server: the NAS sets only MIP6_INTEGRATED, so the server allocates the HA and returns it in MIP6-Agent-Info.
  • Either one: the NAS offers a local HA and the server also returns one and authorizes local assignment. Which the mobile node gets depends on local ASP policy. If the server refuses local assignment, it returns the feature vector with the local bit unset and the HA it allocated.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the front desk picks your home base, sometimes the head office picks it, and sometimes both offer one and the desk chooses.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
MIP6-Agent-Info is allocated code 486 from the normal Diameter AVP code space (values 256 and above). MIP6-Feature-Vector (124) and MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix (125) come from the RADIUS attribute type space (0 to 255) so they stay RADIUS backward-compatible.

IANA created a new Mobility Capability registry holding the two flags. New values must be powers of two (2^x with x of 2 or more) and are assigned by the Specification Required policy of RFC 5226. No way to mark entries deprecated is planned.
sections.eli5: The memo asks for official numbers for its new boxes and starts a public list of the switches, so nobody reuses a switch for something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC adds little security text of its own. The considerations for the integrated scenario are in a companion draft, and those of the Diameter base protocol (RFC 3588), the NASREQ application (RFC 4005) and the Diameter EAP application (RFC 4072) apply.

Developers should take particular care configuring the security associations that protect the messages used to allocate home agents. When messages cross AAA brokers or Diameter agents, the NAS-to-server communication relies on the security properties of those intermediaries.
sections.eli5: Home base choices travel through helpers, so you must trust the helpers and keep the messages locked.
